questions.q: In plain words, what does Fivetran do for you?
options: It builds your dashboards and reports
It stores your only copy of the data for safekeeping
It copies data from your apps and databases into a warehouse or lake and keeps it fresh
It cleans and models the data so your team never has to write SQL
questions.explain: You pick a source, a destination and a schedule, and Fivetran runs the connector. The reshaping afterwards, usually in SQL, is still your job.

questions.q: A new connection finishes its first big copy. What does it do from then on?
options: It copies every table again, every time
It moves only what was changed or added, on a schedule
It waits until you start the next copy by hand
It deletes the source data once it is safely copied
questions.explain: The first run is the initial sync and copies everything you selected. After that it switches to incremental mode and moves only the changes.

questions.q: In the post's orders example, one order is deleted in the source database. What does the destination show afterwards?
options: The order is gone, so reports match the source on their own
The whole table is copied again from scratch
The order moves into a separate archive folder
The order is still there, just marked as deleted
questions.explain: Order 3 stays in the destination, flagged as deleted. Your queries need to filter flagged rows out, or deleted orders sneak into your reports.

questions.q: A database keeps its change log for a limited time. What happens if Fivetran falls behind for longer than that?
options: It has to copy the whole source again, because the record of what changed is gone
Nothing, it quietly picks up where it left off
It guesses the missing changes from the old copy
It switches your plan to a cheaper tier
questions.explain: Think of the log as a diary the database wipes after a while. If Fivetran misses the window, the changes are gone, so the fix is a full re-copy. Big tables mean extra load and extra waiting.

questions.q: Fivetran bills by monthly active rows, counted per connection. Which setup costs more at the same list rates?
options: One connection with 4 million changed rows
They cost the same, since the total is 4 million either way
Four connections with 1 million changed rows each
It depends only on how many users you add
questions.explain: Each connection is priced on its own curve and you can't pool them. The post's Standard-plan example is about $1,010 for one 4 million row connection, against $2,000 for four 1 million row ones.
